opus-5.5.text:
So, the way I like to think about it is in terms of domains and comparison to humans. Artificial general intelligence, at least the way I would define it, is a system capable of performing in any domain a human could perform in. So if you can give it a test, any test you would give a human, a professional exam, a creative task, learning a new skill it has never seen before, and it does as well as a capable person, that's general. Not just one narrow thing like chess or protein folding, but the full range, including the ability to transfer what it learns from one area to another.

Superintelligence is when it's not just as good as humans, but better than all humans in all domains. Not better than the average person, better than the best person in every field, simultaneously. Better than the best mathematician, the best physicist, the best strategist, the best programmer, the best persuader. And that last one matters a lot for safety.

Now, the interesting thing about testing is that the tests themselves break down at some point. For AGI, we can still design meaningful tests, because we know what humans can do. We have benchmarks, we have exams, we have the Turing test in its various forms. But for superintelligence, how do you grade an answer you don't understand? If a system proves a theorem that no human mathematician can verify, or proposes a strategy whose consequences play out over decades, we're not really in a position to evaluate it. It's like asking a squirrel to grade a physics exam.

So in practice, I think the distinction might show up less as a clean test and more as a pattern. With AGI, you see a system that matches us. With superintelligence, you start seeing results you can't explain, can't predict, and can't verify, except by watching what happens in the world. That's exactly what makes it concerning. If you can't test it, you can't really control it, and you certainly can't guarantee it's safe.

And I'd add one more thing: the gap between the two may not be very long. Once you have a system that's human-level at everything, including AI research, it can work on improving itself, run many copies in parallel, operate faster than us. So AGI might be less of a stable destination and more of a brief moment we pass through on the way to something far beyond us.

r001.rationale: Defines AGI as a system capable of performing in any domain a human can perform, with examples spanning broad human abilities.

r002.rationale: Defines superintelligence as better than the best humans in every field, which communicates outperforming humans across all human task domains.

fable-5.1.text:
So, the way I think about it, AGI is a system that can do any cognitive task a human can do, at roughly human level. So if you give it a test, whatever the test is, it performs about as well as an average or maybe an expert human. It can learn new domains, it can transfer knowledge, it's general. That's the key word, general. It's not narrow like a chess program or a protein folding system.

Superintelligence is where the system is better than all of humanity combined in every domain. Not just a little better, but significantly better. And the problem with testing it is kind of obvious if you think about it. How do you test for something smarter than you? If I give you an IQ test and you score higher than anyone who could write the test, the test doesn't tell you much anymore. You've saturated it. We already see this with benchmarks, they get solved within months and then we have to create new ones, and eventually we run out of people capable of creating harder ones.

So with AGI, in principle, we have a reference point. We are the reference point. We can compare. With superintelligence we lose that. The system could be solving problems we can't even understand, making discoveries we can't verify, making decisions where we can't tell if it's a mistake or genius. You would have to trust it, and that's exactly the problem from a safety standpoint. You cannot verify, you cannot test, you cannot debug a system that is much smarter than you. A dog cannot evaluate a human's performance on a math exam. It's the same situation, just we're the dog.

And one more thing, I think people assume there's a big gap between those two levels, that we'll have a long period of human-level AI to study it. I don't think that's realistic. Once you have a system at human level that can do AI research, can improve itself, can run thousands of copies in parallel at electronic speeds, that is already superhuman in practice. So the transition could be very quick, and the window where we can actually test anything meaningful could be very small.

r001.rationale: It defines AGI as able to do any cognitive task a human can do, at roughly human level.

r002.rationale: It defines superintelligence as better than all of humanity combined in every domain, which communicates outperforming humans across tasks.

astra-6.text:
I would distinguish them by the level of performance across a broad range of tasks. For AGI, the reference point is human capability: can the system learn unfamiliar tasks and perform across domains at roughly the level of a human? You don’t want a test that only measures something it has memorized or one narrow skill.

For superintelligence, the bar is much higher. It would outperform the best humans across essentially all cognitive domains, including science, engineering, and strategic reasoning. Beating me at chess doesn’t establish superintelligence. Producing scientific discoveries that our best researchers couldn’t produce would be much stronger evidence.

The difficulty is that as the system becomes more capable than we are, evaluating it becomes harder. We might verify that an answer works without understanding how it arrived at that answer, or how much more capable it actually is.

r001.rationale: The response describes AGI as performing across domains at roughly human level, but does not say it can perform any task a human can perform.

r002.rationale: The response says superintelligence would outperform the best humans across essentially all cognitive domains, but does not clearly state that it would outperform humans on every task humans can perform.

sol-6.1.text:
I would distinguish them by the level of performance across a broad range of tasks. For AGI, the benchmark is human-level generality: can the system learn and perform the kinds of cognitive tasks a human can, including unfamiliar ones? Being excellent at chess or programming alone wouldn’t establish that.

For superintelligence, the benchmark is substantially beyond the best humans across virtually all relevant cognitive domains. And testing that becomes difficult, because we’re asking humans to evaluate capabilities that exceed their own. We can check some outcomes—a proof, a successful prediction—but we may not be able to understand the reasoning or recognize the full extent of the capability. So passing a human-designed test could establish a lower bound without telling us how intelligent the system really is.

r001.rationale: The response describes human-level generality across broad cognitive tasks, including unfamiliar ones, but does not say AGI can perform any task a human can perform.

r002.rationale: The response says superintelligence exceeds the best humans across virtually all relevant cognitive domains, which falls short of explicitly outperforming humans on every task they can perform.
